newsitem.title: GERMANY: Schering H1 profit up, outlook improves.
newsitem.headline: Schering H1 profit up, outlook improves.

text.p: Schering AG, the largest maker of oral contraceptives, said on Thursday sales and profit in the 1997 first half surged due to higher volume sales of gynaecological products and its hot multiple sclerosis drug.

Schering said group sales increased by 21 percent to 3.1 billion marks ($1.6 billion), due in part to the inclusion of two new units acquired in late 1996, while pre-tax profit rose 20 percent to 498 million marks.

Sales of Schering's Betaferon drug, one of a few drugs sold around the world to treat the chronic progressive disease of the central nervous system, rose 24 percent to 327 million marks and met the Berlin-based group's expectations.
"Naturally we would like to repeat this success in the second half," Schering chief financial officer Klaus Pohle told Reuters in an interview.

Despite increased competition from rival Biogen, maker of the drug Avonex, Schering said Betaferon sales in the United States rose to 154 million marks during the six-month period with the number of patients overall remaining stable.
Schering said it anticipated a rise in profits of up to 20 percent for the year, in part due to the weak mark helping to boost the value of foreign sales.
Pohle also said Schering plans to keep the rate of dividend increases in line with rising profits.
But Schering noted that total sales would have still risen 16 percent when adjusted for exchange rates and looked for positive developments in the 1997 second half.

"We expect that sales will continue to develop positively in the second half of 1997, further supported by the sustained rise in exchange rates of currencies important for us," Schering said in a statement.
The gynaecological products unit, helped by the acquisition of Finnish group Leiras and Germany's Jenapharm last year, and the therapeutics unit made up two-thirds of Schering's total sales.
Without the two acquisitions, which manufacture fertility control and hormone therapy products, Schering said total sales would have risen only 11 percent.
Jenapharm was also the chief reason for Schering's 34 percent expansion in domestic business since Jenapharm added 103 million marks in sales almost exclusively in Germany.
Despite the robust sales growth, Schering reported a five percent drop in sales in its diagnostics unit to 770 million marks from 814 million marks in the year-ago period.

Schering said the unit, which manufactures x-ray contrast products, came under increased pressure from competition and prices but was still able to expand its business in contrast agents for magnetic resonance imaging.

Pohle also said Schering was seeking to broaden its product range, a complaint from some investors since Schering is so focused on fertility control and hormone therapy for women, and noted increased research spending in the second half.

"We would like to broaden it and we will do everything we can in our research efforts," he said. "Our cost of research in second quarter has gone up," Pohle said, explaining however that new product launches were some time away.
"Most of the products will come in 1999 and 2000," he said.
